statement: I can describe what we currently know and don't know about 2026-XJ, and identify what physics tools I would need to learn more.
I can use precise vocabulary (position, distance, displacement) to describe motion, and I can tell the difference between scalar and vector quantities.
I can capture a position–time graph with a Vernier motion detector and explain what its slope tells me about velocity.
I can read a velocity-time graph and break a 2-D velocity into its toward-Earth and perpendicular components.
I can use velocity and time to predict an object's future position, and I can express uncertainty in a prediction.
I can add two vectors tip-to-tail and break a vector into components with simple trig.
I can define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity and calculate it from velocity-time data.
I can pick and use the right equation of motion for a constant-acceleration problem.
I can explain Newton's 1st Law in my own words and find everyday examples of inertia.
I can identify the types of force in a scenario (gravity, normal, friction, applied, tension) and draw them as arrows.
I can measure how acceleration changes when I change mass at constant force.
I can measure how acceleration changes when I change the force at constant mass — and combine it with Day 11 to get F = ma.
I can use F = ma to solve problems — always finding the NET force first.
I can identify Newton's 3rd Law force pairs and explain why they don't cancel.
I can draw a free body diagram showing all forces on one object, with arrows sized to the forces.
I can find the net force on an object from its FBD and use it to find acceleration.
I can explain friction as a force that depends on the surfaces and the normal force, and tell static from kinetic friction.
I can recognize when ΣF = 0 and use that to find an unknown force.
I can find my own weak spots from Unit 1 and work to fix them before the transfer task.
I can explain inertia as a mass's resistance to a change in motion, and argue why 2026-XJ's large mass is the obstacle to deflecting it.
I can carry a constant-acceleration model into a new context and state what it can — and cannot yet — predict about 2026-XJ.
I can interrogate F = ma — name the hidden assumptions (constant force, fixed mass) and the conditions under which they break.
I can defend an equilibrium claim (ΣF = 0) and state the assumptions it rests on.
I can justify my choice of axes when decomposing forces on an incline, and name the assumptions behind the result.
I can connect kinematics and forces as one chain — net force to acceleration to motion.
I can defend my reasoning aloud using claim-evidence-reasoning.
I can locate Unit 1 in the year's arc — name what it cannot yet answer and which unit will.
I can state my modeling assumptions and connect my analysis across the unit on the transfer task.
I can explain why 2026-XJ's velocity won't stay constant and name the force that bends its path.
I can describe free fall as constant acceleration g, read g from a v–t slope, and calculate fall times for short drops.
I can distinguish mass from weight and use F = mg to find weight for any local g.
I can write F = G·m₁·m₂/r², explain each symbol, and explain why gravitation is universal and inverse-square.
I can compute the gravitational force between two masses using scientific notation.
I can reason about how F scales when mass or distance changes (r×2 → F×¼; r×½ → F×4).
I can explain g as gravitational field strength (N/kg) and compute g(r) = G·M/r² at any distance.
I can compare g across altitudes and bodies, and explain orbital weightlessness as free fall — not absent gravity.
I can measure g from the slope of a Vernier v–t graph and identify credible sources of error.
I can decompose projectile motion into independent horizontal and vertical pieces linked only by time.
I can solve horizontal-launch problems: fall time from height first, then horizontal range.
I can decompose an angled launch into components and predict flight time and range, including why 45° maximizes range.
I can compute a_c = v²/r and F_c = m·v²/r and identify which force plays the centripetal role.
I can explain an orbit as continuous free fall and derive v_orbit = √(G·M/r).
I can state Kepler's three laws and use T² = a³ for Sun-orbits.
I can apply gravitation and Kepler's laws to predict 2026-XJ's period, perihelion, and orbit crossings.
I can apply every Unit 2 tool — gravitation, fields, projectiles, circular motion, orbits, Kepler — independently on the transfer task.
I can name the two things that make a moving object hard to stop and frame the two Unit 3 questions about 2026-XJ.
I can compute p = m·v with correct units and use momentum as a vector with signed velocities.
I can derive FΔt = Δp from F = ma and use the impulse-momentum theorem.
I can compute momentum, Δp, and impulse, and find force from Δp and Δt.
I can explain why extending Δt reduces F for the same Δp and apply it to safety devices and follow-through.
I can state conservation of momentum and its no-net-external-force condition, and solve recoil problems.
I can distinguish elastic, inelastic, and perfectly inelastic collisions and which conservation laws apply to each.
I can run Vernier cart collisions, compute Σp before and after, and report % difference with a credible error source.
I can solve a 1D perfectly inelastic collision with correct signs and units.
I can solve a 1D elastic collision, including the equal-mass and one-at-rest special cases.
I can apply conservation of momentum separately to x- and y-components and solve a 2D glancing collision.
I can compute a DART-style Δv and reason about asteroid deflection using Δv × lead time.
I can compute an asteroid impact's average force and explain why Earth's velocity change is negligible while the local force is catastrophic.
I can run a full 2026-XJ analysis on both branches (deflection and impact) and articulate which unit ideas were load-bearing.
I can apply every Unit 3 tool independently on the transfer task.
I can articulate why momentum gave us force but not damage, and predict that something involving speed-squared does the work.
I can compute work W = F·d in joules and identify when a force does work.
I can compute work at an angle (W = F·d·cos θ) and identify negative and zero work.
I can compute KE = ½mv² and explain why doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy.
I can apply the work-energy theorem W_net = ΔKE to solve problems.
I can measure speed with photogates and verify the work-energy theorem within a % difference.
I can compute gravitational PE near Earth with U = mgh from a stated reference height.
I can explain when U = mgh fails (g changes with altitude) and read a g-vs-altitude curve.
I can use universal PE, U = −GMm/r, and interpret its negative sign.
I can state conservation of mechanical energy (KE + PE = constant) and its no-friction condition.
I can solve conservation problems for rolling, sliding, and swinging objects.
I can analyze a roller coaster and a pendulum with the energy ledger, including v = √(2gΔh).
I can run the Vernier ramp lab and verify v² is proportional to release height.
I can use Hooke's law F = −kx and interpret the spring constant k.
I can compute spring PE = ½kx² and use it in energy conservation problems.
I can compute power P = W/t = F·v in watts and distinguish energy from power.
I can compute the KE lost in inelastic collisions and verify KE conservation in elastic ones.
I can account for 'missing' mechanical energy as heat and trace full energy chains.
I can convert an impactor's kinetic energy to TNT-equivalent yield and place it on the impact scale.
I can derive and use escape velocity v_esc = √(2GM/r) for any body.
I can run the three-branch energy budget for 2026-XJ and defend the conclusion.
I can apply every Unit 4 tool independently on the transfer task.
I can distinguish thermal energy (total molecular KE), temperature (average per molecule), and heat (thermal energy that transfers).
I can compute heat with Q = m·c·ΔT and interpret specific heat as a material property.
I can distinguish conduction, convection, and radiation and identify each in real scenarios.
I can compute phase-change heat with Q = m·L and read a heating curve's plateaus.
I can run a Vernier calorimetry experiment and identify a metal from its measured specific heat.
I can explain temperature as average molecular kinetic energy using kinetic theory.
I can apply the first law ΔU = Q − W with correct signs.
I can state the second law, explain why heat flows hot to cold, and reason about entropy.
I can analyze a heat engine's energy flow and compute its efficiency.
I can explain why small rocks burn up on atmospheric entry and reason about the size threshold.
I can partition impact energy into thermal components and build a damage-by-distance map.
I can apply every Unit 5 tool independently on the transfer task.
I can explain that waves carry energy, not matter, and frame how RADAR measured everything we know about 2026-XJ.
I can label and compute wave anatomy: frequency, wavelength, amplitude, and period.
I can use the wave equation v = fλ to solve for any of the three quantities.
I can apply the law of reflection and describe wave behavior at boundaries.
I can explain refraction as speed change at a boundary and predict which way a wave bends.
I can describe diffraction around obstacles and how it depends on wavelength vs. opening size.
I can predict constructive and destructive interference and explain standing waves.
I can describe sound as a longitudinal pressure wave with compressions and rarefactions.
I can reason about the speed of sound in different media and explain resonance and harmonics.
I can measure the speed of sound with an echo timing experiment and report % error.
I can reason about intensity, decibels, and the Doppler shift of a moving source.
I can place EM bands on the spectrum and use c = fλ for light.
I can locate virtual images in plane mirrors using the law of reflection.
I can qualitatively describe how converging and diverging lenses form images.
I can walk the full radar measurement chain: pulse timing → distance, Doppler shift → velocity, signal strength → size.
I can use Wien's law to connect meteor color to temperature.
I can reason about seismic waves and tsunami formation, shoaling, and damage at distance.
I can apply every Unit 6 tool independently on the transfer task.
I can describe charge as Unit 7's fundamental quantity, distinguish positive from negative, and name where the unit is heading — including the bridge to the Car Project.
I can compute the electric force with Coulomb's law F = kq₁q₂/r² and reason about its inverse-square scaling.
I can describe an electric field qualitatively and read field-line diagrams.
I can explain voltage as energy per charge and compute it from energy and charge.
I can compute current I = q/t and describe what physically flows in a wire.
I can use Ohm's law V = IR to solve for any of the three quantities.
I can analyze series circuits: equivalent resistance, shared current, and voltage division.
I can analyze parallel circuits: branch currents, shared voltage, and reduced equivalent resistance.
I can reduce and solve combination circuits step by step.
I can wire and measure real circuits with ammeter and voltmeter and verify Ohm's law and the series/parallel rules.
I can compute electric power P = VI and relate it to resistor heating.
I can describe magnetic fields, poles, and Earth's magnetic field.
I can describe how a current creates a magnetic field and predict a solenoid's polarity.
I can explain Faraday induction: a changing magnetic flux induces a voltage.
I can trace the energy flow of motors and generators and compute motor efficiency.
I can explain how Earth's dynamo makes the magnetosphere and reason about EMP effects from an impact.
I can connect every unit of the year to a Car Project component and pre-compute the car's circuit.
I can apply every Unit 7 tool independently on the transfer task.
I can identify the four components of a simple DC circuit (battery, switch, motor, wires) and explain what each does.
I can describe the energy chain that turns a 9V battery into car motion: chemical → electrical → mechanical-rotational → mechanical-translational kinetic.
I can name the relationship a gear pair creates between motor RPM and axle RPM (and the inverse trade with torque).
I can name the physical cause of a car veering left or right (asymmetric friction creating a torque about a vertical axis).
I can predict, using ratio reasoning, how a change in wheel diameter would change my car's top speed and starting effort.
I can justify my chosen wheel set with a written prediction about race performance versus its alternatives.
I can compare what I observed on race day to what I predicted on Day 3, and explain any difference physically.
I can explain three physics choices in my car (wheel size, alignment work, circuit wiring) and what would have happened if I'd chosen differently.
I can build a functional series circuit on PhET (battery → switch → motor stand-in).
I can produce a clean soldered joint on scrap leads.
I can produce a clean soldered joint on the actual car wiring.
I can install axles parallel enough that the car rolls straight for ≥3 m without power.
I can install a switch without breaking the chassis.
I can measure my car's axle RPM by timing a known-distance run and back-calculating from wheel circumference.
I can execute my chosen theme as a finished aesthetic on a working car.
I can identify the build-space safety zones and the safe-handling rule for each tool I will use.
I can commit to a car theme and justify how it fits the project constraints and my build plan.
I can transfer my chassis design to material and make accurate, safe cuts following the build steps.
